On 27 November 2026, I gave the talk "Who Speaks for Learners? Speech AI, Minoritized Languages and the Limits of EU Law" at [AI & Marginalized Knowledge Systems](https://itatsulab.jp/2026/11/09/ai-marginalized-knowledge-systems/), a hybrid workshop at the University of Tokyo.

This was the second workshop in the series run by the Center for Research and Practice in Cultural Continuity at the University of Warsaw, where I sit on the board, this time co-hosted with Yuko Itatsu's lab in Tokyo. The first was [in Warsaw in June](../2026-06-09-marginalized-knowledge-systems-warsaw/index.qmd), where I gave *Who Governs the Spoken Word?*

Speech recognition and synthetic voices for minoritized languages are trained almost entirely on fluent adult speakers. That leaves out the people who actually keep these languages going: learners, children, new speakers. I looked at the gap through two cases, Frisian in the Netherlands and Irish in AAC assistive technology. Then I turned to the law. EU AI law gives rights to individuals and duties to providers. A community harmed as a community has no clear remedy. It's the problem I raised at [Ege University](../2026-11-04-standing-to-be-heard-ege-university/index.qmd) earlier this month, seen this time from the learner's side.

I was in good company. Justyna Olko spoke on equity in digital tools built with Indigenous communities, Asuka Ando on collecting Japanese Sign Language data as a CODA researcher, Matthew Guay on AI for Yaeyaman, and Xinqi He on what large language models do to language itself.

Thanks to Yuko Itatsu and her lab for hosting.
